headline: Massachusetts lacks required racial-profiling traffic-stop reports after funding dispute
dek: The public safety office has not issued the annual analyses since 2024, while officials weigh a new contract that could cost up to $1 million.
body: Massachusetts has gone without the annual public analyses meant to identify racial disparities in traffic stops since 2024, leaving lawmakers and residents without a current statewide review of police citation patterns. The gap surfaced at an Oct. 7 Senate Post Audit and Oversight Committee hearing, where the state’s public safety secretary said the office is still trying to find a workable way to pay for and commission the research.

The reporting requirement comes from the state’s hands-free driving law and is described in [Massachusetts General Laws chapter 90, section 63](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/mass-general-laws-c90-ss-63). The Registry of Motor Vehicles collects demographic information tied to motor-vehicle citations, and the Executive Office of Public Safety and Security, or EOPSS, is required to send the data each year to a Massachusetts university, nonprofit or other institution experienced in analyzing it. The resulting analysis and a public aggregate report are supposed to be posted online without identifying individual drivers or officers.

The system is narrower than a count of every police encounter. Its core data come from traffic stops that produce citations, although the law requires additional information about all traffic stops for a year if the analysis suggests that an agency may have engaged in racial or gender profiling. That follow-up would include the reason for the stop and would be paired with implicit-bias training, according to the statute. The law also calls for public hearings after an annual analysis is received.

Massachusetts has released two rounds of independent work. A report on 2020 data was published in 2022, and a combined analysis of 2021 and 2022 data was released in 2024 by research teams from Salem State University and Worcester State University, according to [EOPSS’s official report archive](https://www.mass.gov/lists/independent-massachusetts-motor-vehicle-uniform-citation-data-analysis-and-report). The second report examined 1,270,129 unique traffic stops and 1,358,720 citations. State officials cautioned that agencies identified as showing potential disparities were not thereby proven to be engaging in racial profiling; the findings were intended to prompt closer examination.

EOPSS Secretary Gina Kwon told the committee that the newest procurement has been difficult because the bids have exceeded what the office can afford. WBUR, reporting for the State House News Service, said the first research contract cost about $300,000 over three years, while proposals in 2025 and 2026 ranged from roughly $600,000 to $1 million. The reporting mandate was created without a dedicated funding stream, so the agency has had to look within its operating budget or find another source of support.

Cost is not the only unresolved issue. Kwon said the office has not found one universally accepted way to analyze the data, and she pointed to criticism of the earlier methodology, including questions about how to identify the driving population and the omission of stops that ended with verbal warnings. The ACLU of Massachusetts told [WBUR](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/13/massachusetts-traffic-stop-race-report-cost-eops) that the analysis should be genuinely independent and argued that traffic stops are one of the most common ways residents encounter police. Those are disagreements about how to measure disparities, not evidence that any particular department currently is or is not profiling drivers.

EOPSS said data collection is continuing and that it is evaluating funding options. The office issued a May solicitation seeking a partner to conduct yearly analyses of state and local motor-vehicle citations and prepare an annual report. The state’s fiscal 2026 public-safety budget exceeded $1.6 billion, but that total covers a broad set of agencies and programs and does not establish that money is available for this contract. No date for the next report was announced at the hearing.

The practical consequence is that 2024 remains the latest publicly posted analysis even as traffic-stop practices and policing priorities change. A new report could give communities, lawmakers and police agencies a comparable baseline, but its conclusions will depend on the research design and the quality of the underlying citation data. Under chapter 90, section 63, once the analysis is received the state must make it public and hold at least three hearings within 30 days. For now, the next step is a funding and procurement decision, followed by the overdue analysis itself.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts traffic-stop racial-profiling reports remain overdue
seoDescription: Massachusetts has not issued required racial-profiling traffic-stop analyses since 2024 as officials weigh research costs and methodology.
